DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

The author's case for the paper:
- **Real data:** two months of till data, a competitor price check, and current supplier information.
- **Modest increases:** each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices, and 60% repeat guests can absorb the rise.
- **Clear gain:** £810 a week (about £42,000 a year), lifting main-course margin to about 71%.
- **Risotto:** it has the weakest margin and lowest sales, so replacing it is an easy improvement.
- **Monitoring:** eight weeks of tracking gives early warning if volumes fall.

The price increases themselves are well justified. But **the risotto proposal rests on a misreading of Table 1**, and **the projected gain leaves out the beef price rise reported in the paper's own Section 4**.

## 1. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu

From Table 1:

| Dish | Gross margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%** (highest) | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |
| Specials | 64% | — |

The paper and the author both say the risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu". Table 1 shows it has the strongest. This is settled. Its sales are the lowest, but tied with specials at 90 plates.

The proposed replacement may make things worse. If the new seasonal special earns at the specials' average margin of 64%, it would make about £8.96 a plate at £14 instead of £11.20. That is about **£200 a week less**, if volumes are similar. If the risotto is the only vegetarian main among the regular dishes, removing it could also lose bookings from groups that include a vegetarian.

The case for removing it would need a different argument, for example that a better vegetarian dish would sell more. That argument isn't in the paper.

## 2. The projected gain leaves out the beef increase

Section 4 reports that **beef prices rise 12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 counts the full £810 a week as additional profit without allowing for it.

The most the beef rise could cost, if the whole food cost of the burger and steak were beef:
- Burger: £4.20 × 12% ≈ £0.50 × 260 plates ≈ **£131 a week**
- Steak: £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 × 120 plates ≈ **£150 a week**

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Gain from price rises (paper) | £810 | £42,120 |
| Beef cost increase (most it could be) | −£281 | −£14,600 |
| **Net gain (at least)** | **≈ £529** | **≈ £27,500** |

The true figure lies between about £27,500 and £42,000. It is probably nearer the lower end, because steak is almost entirely beef. A burger also has a bun and sides, so its cost won't rise the full 12%.

The margin claim changes in the same way. For the five listed dishes, the main-course margin is about **70% now**. The price rises alone would take it to about 71%. **Once the beef increase is included, it stays at about 70%.** In practice, the increases mostly absorb the beef rise rather than rebuild margin.

## 3. The eight-week monitoring is compared with a quiet-season baseline

Sales for April and May will be compared with **January and February**, normally the quietest months. Spring trade usually picks up, so plates sold could rise even if the price increase cost some customers. The monitoring would then miss the problem it is meant to catch.

Compare with **the same weeks last year** instead, or at least compare the three dishes' share of total mains, which seasonal changes affect less.

The paper should also estimate the break-even point. At the new prices, and allowing for beef, the three dishes earn about £8,700 a week in gross profit. **A fall of roughly 6% in their sales would wipe out the net gain**, if those customers leave rather than switch to another dish. Customers who leave also stop buying drinks and desserts. That gives a concrete threshold to monitor against.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday (five days). The conclusion says "six trading days a week". The weekly figures are measured, so the annual totals are unaffected, but correct the text.
- **"Remain the value option."** The prices stay below the midpoint, which is correct (£17.50 vs £17.98, £16.00 vs £16.50, £28.00 vs £29.50). But the restaurant would **no longer be the cheapest** for any of the three dishes, since competitors' lowest prices are £16.95, £15.50 and £27.00. Saying "remains mid-range or lower" would be accurate.
- **Repeat customers.** A 60% repeat rate shows loyalty. It also means most customers know the old prices and will notice the change. Count it as mixed evidence, not reassurance.
- **The 2024 price change** had "no visible effect on bookings". But bookings don't show whether customers switched to cheaper dishes, which plates-per-dish data would. Check that data if it's available.

## What holds up

- **The case for raising prices is sound.** Food margin has fallen from 70% to 67%, prices haven't changed since September 2024, beef is rising, and competitors are charging more. Not raising prices would be the riskier choice.
- **Table 1 arithmetic** is correct: every margin, and the 1,050 plates a week total.
- **The midpoint claim** is correct for all three dishes.
- **The gross figures** of £810 and £42,120 are correct before the beef increase.
- **Monitoring at all** is a good idea. It needs a better baseline.

## What is open, and what would settle it

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Real net gain | The burger's beef cost, split from its total food cost |
| Will sales hold? | Weekly plates per dish against the same weeks last year, with a ~6% loss threshold |
| Should risotto go? | Whether it's the only vegetarian main; the planned special's food cost |
| Did the 2024 change shift orders between dishes? | Plates per dish before and after September 2024 |

## Recommendation

**Approve the three price increases.** They are justified and probably needed just to keep up with the beef rise. Restate the expected gain as about £27,500–£42,000 a year, likely towards the lower end, with margin roughly unchanged at 70%.

**Don't remove the risotto on the grounds given.** It is the most profitable dish per pound of sales. If the owners still want to replace it, the replacement should match its margin and still give vegetarian guests a choice.

**Measure the first eight weeks against last year's same weeks**, not January and February.
